[/dfd_heading][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657787022{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][ultimate_spacer height="30" height_on_tabs="30" height_on_tabs_portrait="30" height_on_mob_landscape="30" height_on_mob="30"][vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][vc_column_text css_animation="bounceIn" css=""]

Every dataset walks in with a question, and every chart type answers a different one. Comparing categories, tracking change, mapping geography, tracing flows; pick the right visualization type and the audience does almost no work at all.

Pick the wrong one and even good analysis reads like static.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][vc_column_text css_animation="bounceIn" css=""]

This guide covers the 15 most common types of data visualization we use in client work, grouped into five chart families, then rounds out the picture with the five delivery formats and five tools that dominate the field.

Each entry says what the type is best at and where it falls over.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width="1/3"][vc_column_text css_animation="bounceIn"]

We built this list from a decade of workshops and studio projects. Skim the family bands, steal the “best for” lines for your next planning meeting, and if events are more your thing, our data visualization conferences guide pairs nicely with it.

MULTIDIMENSIONAL CHARTS

[/dfd_heading][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap="20" bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][dfd_heading module_animation="transition.fadeIn" style="style_01" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:96|line_height:100|color:%23ffffff" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3" heading_margin="margin-top:20px;"]Pie or Donut Chart[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

Best for: one whole, few parts

family: charts & graphs

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/4"][dfd_single_image image="37170" image_size="custom" image_width="300" image_height="300" hover_style="dfd-image-scale" image_border_radius="10"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="5/12"][vc_column_text]

A pie chart splits a single whole into shares your audience can read in two seconds.

Slice count is the whole game. Keep it to five segments or fewer, lead with the biggest share, and the chart does its job before anyone reads a label. The donut variant frees the centre for a headline number, which is why it survives every design fashion cycle.

Once shares get close in size, human eyes stop judging angles well; a humble bar chart beats it there every time.

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][vc_zigzag color="white" el_width="30"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap="20" bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][dfd_heading module_animation="transition.fadeIn" style="style_01" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:96|line_height:100|color:%23ffffff" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3" heading_margin="margin-top:20px;"]Histogram[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

Best for: the shape of one variable

family: charts & graphs

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="5/12"][vc_column_text]

A histogram shows how one measure is distributed, from the runt of the litter to the outliers.

Salary bands, delivery times, response scores; whenever the question is “what is typical and what is extreme?”, this is the chart. Bars touch because the data is continuous, and the bin width you choose quietly decides the story.

Too few bins hides the pattern, too many turns it to noise, so we test several widths before settling.

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/4"][dfd_single_image image="37092" image_size="custom" image_width="300" image_height="300" hover_style="dfd-image-scale" image_border_radius="10"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][vc_zigzag color="white" el_width="30"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap="20" bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][dfd_heading module_animation="transition.fadeIn" style="style_01" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:96|line_height:100|color:%23ffffff" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3" heading_margin="margin-top:20px;"]Scatter Plot[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

Best for: two measures, hunting a relationship

family: charts & graphs

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/4"][dfd_single_image image="37098" image_size="custom" image_width="300" image_height="300" hover_style="dfd-image-scale" image_border_radius="10"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="5/12"][vc_column_text]

A scatter plot throws every record onto two axes and lets the pattern speak.

Marketing spend against revenue, training hours against error rates; the cloud of dots reveals correlation, clusters and outliers in one view. Colour or size can smuggle in a third variable when the story needs it.

Executives sometimes find raw scatters busy, so we often annotate the two or three dots that carry the argument and let the rest fade to context.

TEMPORAL VISUALIZATIONS

[/dfd_heading][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap="20" bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][dfd_heading module_animation="transition.fadeIn" style="style_01" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:96|line_height:100|color:%23ffffff" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3" heading_margin="margin-top:20px;"]Connected Scatter Plot[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

Best for: two measures moving through time

family: temporal

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="5/12"][vc_column_text]

A connected scatter plot traces how two variables travel together, year by year.

Join the dots of a scatter in date order and the chart becomes a path through time: petrol price against consumption, wages against productivity. Loops and reversals appear that neither line chart could show alone.

It rewards an audience willing to slow down, so we save it for reports and long-form pieces, and give it a guided annotation trail.

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/4"][dfd_single_image image="37167" image_size="custom" image_width="300" image_height="300" hover_style="dfd-image-scale" image_border_radius="10"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][vc_zigzag color="white" el_width="30"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap="20" bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][dfd_heading module_animation="transition.fadeIn" style="style_01" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:96|line_height:100|color:%23ffffff" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3" heading_margin="margin-top:20px;"]Polar Area Diagram[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

Best for: cyclical data with drama

family: temporal

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/4"][dfd_single_image image="37134" image_size="custom" image_width="300" image_height="300" hover_style="dfd-image-scale" image_border_radius="10"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="5/12"][vc_column_text]

The polar area diagram, Florence Nightingale’s rose, wraps time around a circle.

Each wedge is a period, and its area carries the value, which suits data with a built-in cycle: seasonal sales, monthly admissions, wind by compass point. Done well it is one of the most beautiful chart forms in the canon.

Areas are harder to compare than lengths, so we reserve it for stories where mood matters as much as precision.

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][vc_zigzag color="white" el_width="30"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap="20" bg_check="row-background-dark" css=".vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}"][vc_column][dfd_heading module_animation="transition.fadeIn" style="style_01" title_font_options="tag:h2|font_size:96|line_height:100|color:%23ffffff" subtitle_font_options="tag:h3" heading_margin="margin-top:20px;"]Time Series[/dfd_heading][vc_column_text css=""]

Best for: anything measured over time

family: temporal

[/vc_column_text][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][ultimate_spacer height="20" height_on_tabs="20" height_on_tabs_portrait="20" height_on_mob_landscape="20" height_on_mob="20"][/vc_column][vc_column width="1/6"][/vc_column][vc_column width="5/12"][vc_column_text]

The time series line chart is the workhorse of business reporting everywhere.

Revenue by month, users by week, temperature by decade; a line against a dated axis is the fastest route from spreadsheet to insight, and every stakeholder already knows how to read one. Trend, seasonality and shock all show at a glance.

Our rule: label the lines directly and retire the legend, because eyes should never commute between the two.

A cartogram redraws the map so each region’s size reflects its value, geography be damned.

Population, votes, emissions; when land area misleads, the cartogram inflates and shrinks regions until the data sets the proportions. Election coverage leans on it because empty land does not vote.

The distortion is the message, and it startles audiences in a useful way, though it needs a familiar base map to stay readable.

A choropleth shades each region by its value, from pale to saturated.

It is the map everyone has seen: unemployment by state, sales by territory, rainfall by council area. The craft hides in the colour scale and in normalising the data, because raw totals just re-draw population.

Show rates per capita and the map starts saying something true.

A dot distribution map places one dot per event and lets density do the talking.

Customer locations, incident reports, species sightings; thousands of small dots build a texture of concentration no summary statistic can match. John Snow mapped cholera this way in 1854 and the form has not aged.

Its weakness is overplotting in dense centres, which clustering or transparency usually solves.

Customer segments, survey respondents, gene families; the branch heights show how similar the members of each cluster really are, which makes it the defensible way to present a segmentation.

An alluvial diagram pours quantities from stage to stage in braided streams.

Marketing channel to lead to sale, energy source to use, voter movement between elections; the stream widths carry the volumes and the crossings show the churn. It is the chart we get asked about most after a presentation.

Keep the stages to three or four and the categories under a dozen, and it stays legible.

Most charts fall into five working families: multidimensional charts like pies, histograms and scatter plots; temporal charts like time series; maps such as choropleths and cartograms; hierarchical charts like trees and sunbursts; and network diagrams like alluvial and node-link charts. Delivery formats sit on top: infographic reports, dashboards, presentations, interactives and animated videos.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="Which chart type is best for comparing categories?" tab_id="faqviztypes-2-2026"][vc_column_text css=""]

A bar chart wins nearly every time because human eyes judge aligned lengths better than angles or areas. Reach for a pie chart only when the point is a share of one whole with five or fewer slices.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What is the difference between a dashboard and an infographic?" tab_id="faqviztypes-3-2026"][vc_column_text css=""]

A dashboard is a live tool that refreshes with the data and answers how are we tracking right now. An infographic report is a designed narrative, fixed at publication, that walks readers through an argument. Most organisations need both, doing different jobs.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title="What tools do professionals use to build data visualizations?" tab_id="faqviztypes-4-2026"][vc_column_text css=""]

Power BI and Tableau dominate business dashboards, Excel and PowerPoint still carry everyday reporting, Adobe Illustrator handles publication-grade infographics, and After Effects drives animated data videos. The Datalabs Agency trains teams in the first four and produces in all of them.

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657787022{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]
[vc_row_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″][vc_column_text css_animation=”bounceIn” css=””]

Every dataset walks in with a question, and every chart type answers a different one. Comparing categories, tracking change, mapping geography, tracing flows; pick the right visualization type and the audience does almost no work at all.

Pick the wrong one and even good analysis reads like static.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″][vc_column_text css_animation=”bounceIn” css=””]

This guide covers the 15 most common types of data visualization we use in client work, grouped into five chart families, then rounds out the picture with the five delivery formats and five tools that dominate the field.

Each entry says what the type is best at and where it falls over.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][vc_column_inner width=”1/3″][vc_column_text css_animation=”bounceIn”]

We built this list from a decade of workshops and studio projects. Skim the family bands, steal the “best for” lines for your next planning meeting, and if events are more your thing, our data visualization conferences guide pairs nicely with it.

[/vc_column_text]

MULTIDIMENSIONAL CHARTS

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Pie or Donut Chart

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: one whole, few parts

family: charts & graphs

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A pie chart splits a single whole into shares your audience can read in two seconds.

Slice count is the whole game. Keep it to five segments or fewer, lead with the biggest share, and the chart does its job before anyone reads a label. The donut variant frees the centre for a headline number, which is why it survives every design fashion cycle.

Once shares get close in size, human eyes stop judging angles well; a humble bar chart beats it there every time.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Histogram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: the shape of one variable

family: charts & graphs

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A histogram shows how one measure is distributed, from the runt of the litter to the outliers.

Salary bands, delivery times, response scores; whenever the question is “what is typical and what is extreme?”, this is the chart. Bars touch because the data is continuous, and the bin width you choose quietly decides the story.

Too few bins hides the pattern, too many turns it to noise, so we test several widths before settling.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Scatter Plot

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: two measures, hunting a relationship

family: charts & graphs

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A scatter plot throws every record onto two axes and lets the pattern speak.

Marketing spend against revenue, training hours against error rates; the cloud of dots reveals correlation, clusters and outliers in one view. Colour or size can smuggle in a third variable when the story needs it.

Executives sometimes find raw scatters busy, so we often annotate the two or three dots that carry the argument and let the rest fade to context.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1693285985202{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

TEMPORAL VISUALIZATIONS

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Connected Scatter Plot

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: two measures moving through time

family: temporal

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A connected scatter plot traces how two variables travel together, year by year.

Join the dots of a scatter in date order and the chart becomes a path through time: petrol price against consumption, wages against productivity. Loops and reversals appear that neither line chart could show alone.

It rewards an audience willing to slow down, so we save it for reports and long-form pieces, and give it a guided annotation trail.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Polar Area Diagram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: cyclical data with drama

family: temporal

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

The polar area diagram, Florence Nightingale’s rose, wraps time around a circle.

Each wedge is a period, and its area carries the value, which suits data with a built-in cycle: seasonal sales, monthly admissions, wind by compass point. Done well it is one of the most beautiful chart forms in the canon.

Areas are harder to compare than lengths, so we reserve it for stories where mood matters as much as precision.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Time Series

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: anything measured over time

family: temporal

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

The time series line chart is the workhorse of business reporting everywhere.

Revenue by month, users by week, temperature by decade; a line against a dated axis is the fastest route from spreadsheet to insight, and every stakeholder already knows how to read one. Trend, seasonality and shock all show at a glance.

Our rule: label the lines directly and retire the legend, because eyes should never commute between the two.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1693285985202{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

MAPS & 2D AREA

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Cartogram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: geography reweighted by data

family: maps

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A cartogram redraws the map so each region’s size reflects its value, geography be damned.

Population, votes, emissions; when land area misleads, the cartogram inflates and shrinks regions until the data sets the proportions. Election coverage leans on it because empty land does not vote.

The distortion is the message, and it startles audiences in a useful way, though it needs a familiar base map to stay readable.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Choropleth

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: rates and ratios across regions

family: maps

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A choropleth shades each region by its value, from pale to saturated.

It is the map everyone has seen: unemployment by state, sales by territory, rainfall by council area. The craft hides in the colour scale and in normalising the data, because raw totals just re-draw population.

Show rates per capita and the map starts saying something true.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Dot Distribution Map

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: density and spread of events

family: maps

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A dot distribution map places one dot per event and lets density do the talking.

Customer locations, incident reports, species sightings; thousands of small dots build a texture of concentration no summary statistic can match. John Snow mapped cholera this way in 1854 and the form has not aged.

Its weakness is overplotting in dense centres, which clustering or transparency usually solves.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1693285985202{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

HIERARCHICAL CHARTS

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Dendrogram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: showing how things cluster

family: hierarchical

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A dendrogram is a branching tree that records how items group together, step by step.

Customer segments, survey respondents, gene families; the branch heights show how similar the members of each cluster really are, which makes it the defensible way to present a segmentation.

We bring it out when a client asks “why these segments and why five?”, because the answer is drawn right into the branches.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Ring or Sunburst Chart

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: part-to-whole with layers

family: hierarchical

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A sunburst chart nests ring inside ring, one level of the hierarchy per band.

Budget to portfolio to project, category to sub-category to SKU; each ring drills a level deeper while the angles keep every slice in proportion to the whole. It rewards interactive drill-down especially well.

Past three rings the labels crowd, so we prune the hierarchy before we draw it.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Tree Diagram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: structures and decisions

family: hierarchical

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A tree diagram lays out parent-to-child structure in clean descending levels.

Org charts, decision trees, site maps, taxonomies; whenever one thing contains or leads to others, the tree is the least ambiguous picture available. Readers navigate it without instruction.

Wide flat hierarchies fight the page edge, and a horizontal layout usually settles the argument.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1693285985202{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

NETWORK VISUALIZATIONS

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Alluvial Diagram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: flows between stages

family: network

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

An alluvial diagram pours quantities from stage to stage in braided streams.

Marketing channel to lead to sale, energy source to use, voter movement between elections; the stream widths carry the volumes and the crossings show the churn. It is the chart we get asked about most after a presentation.

Keep the stages to three or four and the categories under a dozen, and it stays legible.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Node-Link Diagram

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: who connects to whom

family: network

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A node-link diagram draws entities as dots and relationships as the lines between them.

Stakeholder maps, social graphs, system dependencies; the hubs and bridges jump out the moment the layout settles. Force-directed algorithms do the arranging, and a good one makes structure look inevitable.

Beyond a few hundred nodes it becomes the infamous hairball, and filtering becomes the real design work.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Matrix Chart

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: dense networks, no spaghetti

family: network

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A matrix chart tames a network into a grid, one cell per possible connection.

Where the node-link view melts into spaghetti, the matrix stays calm: rows and columns list the entities and each filled cell marks a link. Sorting the rows well is what reveals the blocks and cliques.

It reads less intuitively at first glance, and it repays the ten seconds of orientation it asks for.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1693285985202{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

FORMATS

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Infographic Report

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: narrative data storytelling

format · flat

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

An infographic report walks a reader through an argument, chart by designed chart.

This is the format the Datalabs Agency is best known for: annual reports, impact summaries and research findings rebuilt as designed narratives where typography, illustration and charts share one grid. A report that people actually read changes what the data achieves.

Think of it as long-form journalism for your numbers.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Dashboard

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: live operational monitoring

format · interactive

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A dashboard keeps the numbers that run a business on one living screen.

Built in Power BI or Tableau, refreshed on schedule, filtered by whoever is looking; the dashboard answers “how are we tracking right now?” without a meeting. The design discipline is ruthless triage, because a dashboard that shows everything monitors nothing.

Our dashboard design work usually starts by deleting half the tiles a team asked for.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Data Presentation

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: the boardroom moment

format · flat

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

A data presentation puts one chart per slide in service of a spoken argument.

The numbers may live in a dashboard, and the decision still happens in a room. Presentation charts need bigger type, fewer series and a headline that states the takeaway, because the audience reads while listening.

We teach this rebuild in our training workshops; it is the fastest visualization skill upgrade most teams can make.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Interactive Data Visualization

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: letting readers explore

format · interactive

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

An interactive visualization hands the reader the controls: filter, hover, drill.

Public data tools, scrolling explainers and explorable models earn attention that static images cannot, because the reader’s own question drives the view. The craft is guiding exploration so every path lands somewhere meaningful.

We keep a gallery of favourites in our interactive data visualization examples if you want the inspiration tour.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Animated Data Video

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: broadcast and social reach

format · motion

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

An animated data video choreographs charts to a script, a voiceover and a clock.

Motion adds the one thing static charts lack: controlled sequence. A bar race, a growing line or a morphing map delivers the story beat by beat, which is why the format dominates social feeds and conference openers.

Every second is designed, so scripts come first and the charts are storyboarded like film.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1693285985202{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

TOOLS & SOFTWARE

[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Tableau

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: visual analysis at depth

tool · bi platform

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

Tableau remains the analyst’s favourite canvas for exploring data visually.

Drag, drop and the chart redraws; that immediacy makes Tableau superb for exploratory analysis and for dashboards with polish. Its calculated fields and level-of-detail expressions go deep once the basics are fluent.

We run Tableau training for teams that own licences and want the skills to match.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Power BI

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: the Microsoft-stack organisation

tool · bi platform

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

Power BI turns the Microsoft ecosystem into a reporting platform.

Tight Excel, Teams and Azure integration makes it the default choice for most corporates, and DAX gives it real analytical muscle. Licensing is the pragmatic reason it wins; the visuals reward a designer’s hand to rise above the defaults.

Much of our workshop teaching happens inside Power BI for exactly that reason.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Adobe Illustrator

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: publication-grade polish

tool · design

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

Illustrator is where charts go to become graphics worth publishing.

BI tools chart data; Illustrator crafts the final artwork: custom annotations, bespoke typography, illustrated context, print-ready output. Most of the infographic work we ship passes through it on the way out the door.

The workflow is chart-from-data first, then refine the vectors, never redraw numbers by eye.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Excel & PowerPoint

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: ubiquity and speed

tool · office

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

Excel and PowerPoint are still where most business charts are born and shown.

Dismissed by purists and installed on every machine on earth; used with intent, the pair produces clean, credible charts in minutes. Defaults are the enemy: gridlines, borders and 3D effects all come off before a chart leaves our studio.

Knowing ten Excel chart moves well beats knowing a hundred badly.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row gap=”20″ bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657851210{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Adobe After Effects

[vc_column_text css=””]

Best for: animated data storytelling

tool · motion

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/4″]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”5/12″][vc_column_text]

After Effects is the engine behind almost every animated data video you have admired.

Keyframes, expressions and plugins move charts with broadcast-quality smoothness, far past what any BI tool can animate. The learning curve is real and so is the payoff on screens that need to impress.

Data drives the animation through templates and expressions, keeping the numbers accurate under all that motion.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/6″][/vc_column][vc_column]
[vc_zigzag color=”white” el_width=”30″]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” css=”.vc_custom_1696657979425{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column]

Which type should your team actually use?

[vc_column_text]

Start from the question, never the chart. Comparing categories points to bars; change over time wants a line; geography earns a map; flows deserve an alluvial. The Datalabs Agency is a Melbourne-based data visualization consultancy founded in 2012 that delivers corporate training workshops (Power BI, Tableau, data storytelling), dashboard design, and BI style guides for clients including Mercedes-Benz, Adidas, and UPS.

When your team wants to make these choices confidently, our data visualization training workshops teach exactly this decision craft, with workshop pricing published openly.

[/vc_column_text]
[/vc_column][/vc_row][vc_row bg_check=”row-background-dark” dfd_enable_overlay=”” css=”.vc_custom_1787200000004{background-color: #2f2e3a !important;}”][vc_column width=”1/4″][/vc_column][vc_column width=”1/2″]

Questions & Answers

TYPES OF DATA VISUALIZATION

[/vc_column_text]
[dfd_accordion style=”style-3″ active_section=”1″ font_size=”18″ tab_title_google_fonts=”yes” tab_title_custom_fonts=”font_family:Arvo%3Aregular%2Citalic%2C700%2C700italic|font_style:700%20bold%20regular%3A700%3Anormal” icon_size=”14″][vc_tta_section title=”What are the main types of data visualization?” tab_id=”faqviztypes-1-2026″][vc_column_text css=””]

Most charts fall into five working families: multidimensional charts like pies, histograms and scatter plots; temporal charts like time series; maps such as choropleths and cartograms; hierarchical charts like trees and sunbursts; and network diagrams like alluvial and node-link charts. Delivery formats sit on top: infographic reports, dashboards, presentations, interactives and animated videos.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”Which chart type is best for comparing categories?” tab_id=”faqviztypes-2-2026″][vc_column_text css=””]

A bar chart wins nearly every time because human eyes judge aligned lengths better than angles or areas. Reach for a pie chart only when the point is a share of one whole with five or fewer slices.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”What is the difference between a dashboard and an infographic?” tab_id=”faqviztypes-3-2026″][vc_column_text css=””]

A dashboard is a live tool that refreshes with the data and answers how are we tracking right now. An infographic report is a designed narrative, fixed at publication, that walks readers through an argument. Most organisations need both, doing different jobs.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_tta_section][vc_tta_section title=”What tools do professionals use to build data visualizations?” tab_id=”faqviztypes-4-2026″][vc_column_text css=””]

Power BI and Tableau dominate business dashboards, Excel and PowerPoint still carry everyday reporting, Adobe Illustrator handles publication-grade infographics, and After Effects drives animated data videos. The Datalabs Agency trains teams in the first four and produces in all of them.
